FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE November 19, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2020-2021-03 At the November 5, 2020 meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate. SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS: COLLEGE OF BUSINESS: Creation of a Business Analytics and Intelligence Minor: See Appendix A The Business Analytics and Intelligence program is to provide students with the opportunity to better integrate data insights into their analyses and decision-making process. The program is also designed to strengthen knowledge from their primary major with advanced business analytics skills. Students will be prepared to bring insights from the large amounts of data to their functional areas such as marketing, finance, supply chain management, accounting among others. Students will specialize in one of the functional areas of business to gain additional skills that will prepare them for data-driven and analytics-based decision making. A minimum of six courses (18 credits) with an overall GPA of 2.0. A GPA of 2.0 (includes all attempts) is mandatory for the minor. Half of the credits for the minor (3 courses) must be completed at URI. All the courses for the minor must be taken at an AACSB accredited business school, at the URI Data Science program (CSC 201 or CSC 211) or through an approved study abroad program. 1

Business Analytics and Intelligence (BAI) is the area of study that deals with skills, technologies, practices for efficient data management, continuous iterative exploration and investigation of business performance to gain insight and drive business planning.
There are an increasing number of BAI tools and methodologies newly introduced to the industry and academia every day.

These tools and methodologies provide field practitioners with statistical and operations analysis, the formation of predictive models, application of optimization techniques, and the communication of these results to customers, business partners, and college executives.
Business Analytics and Intelligence requires quantitative methods and evidence-based data for business modeling and decision making.
Business Analytics and Intelligence provide the industry with a great deal of benefits.
Data management solutions and analytical software continue to proliferate and provide better decision-making tools.
Businesses are increasingly relying on business analytics to gain a competitive advantage or just to keep up with the competition.
As such, students trained with BAI programs are highly-demanding future employees.
According to the U.S.
Bureau of Labor Statistics, Data scientist salaries in the United

States: $130,290 (2017), and Data scientist was ranked at #1 among 50 best jobs in America (Glassdoor.com).
Business analysts often specialize in a particular industry, such as medical science, telecommunications and energy.
Or, they may work in a specific area of business, like marketing, human resources or supply chain management.
In particular, those who are working for smaller firms may serve as general practitioners.
In all settings, the job of these professionals is to define a problem, collect and analyze data pertaining to it, evaluate company processes and procedures, and ultimately recommend and deploy strategies designed to solve the issue.
The Business Analytics and Intelligence program is to provide students with the opportunity to better integrate data insights into their analyses and decision-making process.
The program is also designed to strengthen knowledge from their primary major with advanced business analytics skills.
Students will be prepared to bring insights from the large amounts of data to their functional areas such as marketing, finance, supply chain management, accounting among others.

Students will specialize in one of the functional areas of business to gain additional skills that will prepare them for data-driven and analytics-based decision making.
Many of the courses of the program will be revised to include the important learning goals specific to Business Analytics and Intelligence.
Some courses listed in the COB curriculum will be tailored for BAI students.
The program will offer the courses of business statistics and mathematics, business application programming, data analytics software, e-Commerce, data management and visualization.
These courses were offered for the Management Information Systems (MIS) major in the college of business.
A minimum of six courses (18 credits) with an overall GPA of 2.0.
A GPA of 2.0 (includes all attempts) is mandatory for the minor.
Half of the credits for the minor (3 courses) must be completed at URI.
All the courses for the minor must be taken at an AACSB accredited business school, at the URI Data Science program (CSC 201 or CSC 211) or through an approved study abroad program.

1 FACULTY SENATE OFFICE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE September 17, 2020 Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee Report 2019-2020-12 At the July 28, 2020 special summer meeting of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty Senate.
SECTION II Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation by the Faculty Senate ORGANIZATIONAL CHANGES: COLLEGE OF ARTS AND SCIENCES: Africana Studies Program: See Appendix A To make Africana Studies an academic department rather than a program.
Africana Studies has been a program at the University of Rhode Island for more than three decades.
During that time, Africana Studies (referred to as AAF) has always embodied the values of racial and social justice.
AAF has served in many ways as a moral center of the University regarding issues of equity and fairness.
The curriculum provided by AAF is a mainstay of cultural, social and historical understanding and a critical and defining part of the American narrative, a narrative that is wholly American, not just singularly Black American.

Recent articulation of the transformational goals and mission of the University directly spell out the necessary movement from institutionalized racism to new constructs of diversity (racial and ethnic affirmation for all people) and inclusion.
The proposal for departmental status is not a reactionary idea.
The expectations and goals of AAF have come to far exceed ‘program’ status.
It is critical that AAF be confirmed as a department because AAF needs the designation to create the infrastructure to develop its relevance to our students and build our curriculum.
Departmental status will situate AAF in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding recruit new faculty, recruit students to the major and minor, and enlarge our capacity to respond nationally and globally, in more informed ways, to an increasing demand for justice.

2 Gender and Women’s Studies Program: See Appendix B To make Gender and Women’s Studies an academic department rather than a program. In designating Gender and Women’s Studies (GWS) as a “Department,” URI will affirm that GWS is equal in status and importance to all other Departments at URI. Consistent with the goals outlined in the Academic Strategic Plan (2016-2021), this change will demonstrate unequivocally URI’s commitment to student success, diversity, and social justice—all at the core of GWS teaching and scholarship. Except for being accorded equal status as a “Department,” since 1972, GWS has operated just like other departments. GWS has its own budget, “director” who participates in all chair obligations and duties, growing number of majors (45 in FY2021) and minors, TT, full-time, and joint faculty lines, an endowed chair, URI Foundation funds, student scholarships, sponsored events, and a graduate certificate program that has graduated over 30 students. But it is time now to give GWS equal status.

Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.
Africana Studies has been a program at the University of Rhode Island for more than three decades.
During that time, Africana Studies (referred to as AAF) has always embodied the values of racial and social justice.
AAF has served in many ways as a moral center of the University regarding issues of equity and fairness.
The curriculum provided by AAF is a mainstay of cultural, social and historical understanding and a critical and defining part of the American narrative, a narrative that is wholly American, not just singularly Black American.
Recent articulation of the transformational goals and mission of the University directly spell out the necess ary movement from institutionalized racism to new constructs of diversity (racial and ethnic affirmation for all people) and inclusion.

Given the recent events of George Floyd's tragic death and other killings of Black men and women at the hands of American police officers, our nation is embroiled in a resurgence of racial conflict.
The urgency of this time in history is to re -think our commitments to racial equity.
It is a time for our institution to review policies and practices and confront long-standing institutional racism.
Specifically, URI has begun to respond to these exigencies by confronting the issues of institutional racism through enacting courses of action that are direct and measurable.
As part of that important response, we propose the explicit endorsement of Africana Studies to departmental status.
The proposal for departmental status is not a reactionary idea.
The expectations and goals of AAF have come to far exceed 'program' status.
It is critical that AAF be confirmed as a department because AAF needs the designation to create the infrastructure to develop its relevance to our students and build our curriculum.

Departmental status will situate AAF in a more competitive position to attract internal and external funding recruit new faculty, recruit students to the major and minor, and enlarge our capacity to respond nationally and globally, in more informed ways, to an increasing demand for justice.
As the state's flagship public research institution, the University of Rhode Island is a vibrant and dynamic community that is connected by: a common quest for knowledge to transform the way we perceive and understand the world; a sincere desire for innovation to enrich the campus community and the state of Rhode Island; and a real commitment to embrace social justice and to promote civic engage-ment.
These same connecting principles (i.e., knowledge, innovation, social justice, civic engagement, etc.) are the foundations upon which the Department of Africana Studies were established, over thirty years ago.
